scenes.tts: Of one hundred banded birds, sixty are seen at the colony next year. Did forty die? Not necessarily. Some may be alive and unseen. Some may be breeding at another colony. To say whether a population can replace itself, you first need a clean count of who survives and who reproduces at each age.
scenes.visual: 100 bird dots in a colony box; 60 turn blue (seen), 40 grey; some turn hollow (alive, unseen) and some hop to a second colony box
scenes.narration: Of one hundred banded birds, sixty are seen at the colony next year. Did forty die? Not necessarily. Some may be alive and unseen. Some may be breeding at another colony. To say whether a population can replace itself, you first need a clean count of who survives and who reproduces at each age.

scenes.tts: So start with a cleaner case. A cohort is a group of individuals born together. Follow one from birth, and at each age count how many are still alive. Here is a made-up cohort of females, closed and completely observed. It starts with one hundred. A year later, eighty are alive. Then forty. Then ten. Then none.
scenes.visual: bars for the number alive at ages 0 to 4 grow in one by one and shrink
scenes.narration: So start with a cleaner case. A cohort is a group of individuals born together. Follow one from birth, and at each age count how many are still alive. Here is a made-up cohort of females, closed and completely observed. It starts with one hundred. A year later, eighty are alive. Then forty. Then ten. Then none.

scenes.tts: Divide each count by the starting one hundred, and you get survivorship, the fraction of the cohort still alive. Next, count the deaths in each year. Divide them by the number alive at the start of that year, not by the original one hundred. In the first year, a fifth die. Then half. Then three quarters. Then all. In this cohort, the chance of dying rises with age.
scenes.visual: survivorship labels appear above the bars; red top sections mark the deaths; the red share of each bar reads off the death probability
scenes.narration: Divide each count by the starting one hundred, and you get survivorship, the fraction of the cohort still alive. Next, count the deaths in each year. Divide them by the number alive at the start of that year, not by the original one hundred. In the first year, a fifth die. Then half. Then three quarters. Then all. In this cohort, the chance of dying rises with age.

scenes.tts: Now add the births. Each surviving female gives birth in a single pulse at each age. At age one, eighty females have one daughter each. At age two, forty females have two each. At age three, ten females have one each. That makes eighty plus eighty plus ten. One hundred seventy daughters from one hundred founders.
scenes.visual: green daughter blocks grow beside the bars at ages 1, 2 and 3, then stack into one tall column against a line at 100 founders
scenes.narration: Now add the births. Each surviving female gives birth in a single pulse at each age. At age one, eighty females have one daughter each. At age two, forty females have two each. At age three, ten females have one each. That makes eighty plus eighty plus ten. One hundred seventy daughters from one hundred founders.

scenes.tts: So the net reproductive rate, R nought, is one point seven daughters per newborn female. It is counted per generation, not per year. If the rates stayed fixed, above one means the population grows in the long run. Below one means it declines. At exactly one, it just replaces itself. That is a prediction from assumptions, not an observation.

That is a prediction from assumptions, not an observation.

scenes.tts: A table is only as good as its counts. A bird not seen may be alive and missed, or alive and gone. Missing is not dead. So count the survivors and the births at each age. Survivors and births by age give R nought, and R nought says whether a cohort replaces itself.
